old: Voltage across an inductor is $L\,dI/dt$; in parallel the current splits, so each inductor carries $I/2$
new: Voltage across an inductor is $L\,dI/dt$; in parallel each inductor has the same voltage across it, so $L_1\,dI_1/dt = L_2\,dI_2/dt$ and the current divides inversely as $L$ (each carries $I/2$ only if $L_1 = L_2$)
fixes: Parallel inductors: current divides inversely as L, not always I/2

old: Forgetting that in parallel inductors each carries only part of the current, so the emf across the combination differs from that across one inductor in series.
new: Forgetting how current and emf divide between inductors: in parallel, all inductors have the same emf across them, and the currents divide inversely as $L$. In series, all carry the same current, and the emfs divide in proportion to $L$.
fixes: Replaced misleading parallel/series inductor emf trap

old: In a series LCR circuit driven by $V = V_0\sin\omega t$, the current is $I = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, where $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$. The circuit is inductive if $X_L > X_C$ (current lags) and capacitive if $X_C > X_L$ (current leads). Resonance occurs when $X_L = X_C$, that is $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance Z is minimum and equal to R, the current is maximum ($V_0/R$), $\phi = 0$ and the power factor is 1. $V_L$ and $V_C$ are equal and opposite, cancelling each other, and each may be much larger than the source voltage. Sharpness of resonance is measured by the quality factor $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$. The bandwidth is $\Delta\omega = R/L$. A smaller R gives a sharper resonance. Resonance is used in radio and TV tuning circuits. It needs both L and C to be present.
new: In a series LCR circuit driven by $V = V_0\sin\omega t$, the current is $I = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, where $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$. The circuit is inductive if $X_L > X_C$ (current lags) and capacitive if $X_C > X_L$ (current leads). Resonance occurs when $X_L = X_C$, that is $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance Z is minimum and equal to R, the current is maximum ($V_0/R$), $\phi = 0$ and the power factor is 1. $V_L$ and $V_C$ are equal and opposite, cancelling each other, and each may be much larger than the source voltage. Sharpness of resonance is measured by the quality factor $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$. The bandwidth is $2\Delta\omega = R/L$, so $Q = \omega_0/(2\Delta\omega)$. A smaller R gives a sharper resonance. Resonance is used in radio and TV tuning circuits. It needs both L and C to be present.
